articles.title: Tanker secondhand sales smash records with $30bn changing hands
articles.summary: The extraordinary tanker sale-and-purchase boom has broken another record, with more tonnage changing hands in the first ten months of 2026 than in any previous full year, while secondhand vessel prices have climbed to unprecedented levels. New figures from Clarksons Research show that 588 tankers totalling 69.6m dwt...
articles.body: Tankers Tanker secondhand sales smash records with $30bn changing hands Sam Chambers November 16, 2026 0 49 2 minutes read K Line K Line The extraordinary tanker sale-and-purchase boom has broken another record, with more tonnage changing hands in the first ten months of 2026 than in any previous full year, while secondhand vessel prices have climbed to unprecedented levels. New figures from Clarksons Research show that 588 tankers totalling 69.6m dwt have been reported sold so far this year, already 8% above the previous annual record set in 2022. The combined value of transactions has reached $29.7bn, almost double the $16.2bn recorded throughout 2025. VLCCs have been at the forefront of the buying frenzy, with 124 supertankers changing hands this year compared with 78 during the whole of 2025 with Sinokor leading the charge. The surge has completely upended conventional ship valuations. Clarksons now assesses a five-year-old VLCC at $220m, compared with $120m at the end of last year, while a 10-year-old vessel is valued at $195m, more than double its end-2025 assessment. Even a 15-year-old supertanker is now worth $165m, compared with just $62m last December. A prompt VLCC resale is valued at an astonishing $245m, almost $114m more than the $131.5m benchmark cost of ordering a new vessel. Clarksons’ five-year-old tanker price index has climbed 49% over the past 12 months. Other brokers have documented similarly extraordinary gains. Xclusiv Shipbrokers reported earlier this month that five-year-old VLCC values had increased 80% year-on-year by October, with suezmaxes gaining 64%. The surge in valuations reflects the spectacular freight earnings generated by the war in the Middle East and the premium buyers are willing to pay for vessels available immediately rather than newbuildings delivering in 2029 or later. Clarksons reported that average VLCC spot earnings fell 41% last week to $304,482 a day, although rates remain historically elevated. Meanwhile, the industry’s enormous newbuilding programme is gathering pace, with a record 234 VLCCs ordered this year alone. The risks of buying at today’s extraordinary prices dominated discussions at last month’s Maritime CEO Forum in Monaco. Burak Cetinok, head of research at Arrow, calculated that VLCC earnings were running at 14 times their 10-year average, warning that once orderbooks reach 25% of the existing fleet, earnings have historically declined within 24 to 36 months. Alan Hatton, chief executive of Foreguard Shipping, cautioned against making a “one-way directional bet” on continued market strength, particularly with expensive newbuildings delivering in 2030 or later. DHT boss Svein Moxnes Harfjeld was more optimistic, noting that almost half the VLCC fleet would be over 15 years old by 2029. articles.body: Gulftainer has announced a partnership with MSC, through Terminal Investment Limited (TiL), and PT Karya Citra Nusantara (KCN) to develop a new international container terminal at Marunda Port in Jakarta, Indonesia. The proposed terminal will have an annual handling capacity of up to 2.2 million TEUs. According to Gulftainer, the development is expected to become the largest single container terminal in Jakarta and Indonesia. The project brings together Gulftainer, MSC’s terminal investment arm and Indonesian port operator KCN. The partnership aims to expand container-handling infrastructure and support international trade through Jakarta. Gulftainer described the development as a long-term commitment to Indonesia’s trade infrastructure, industrial competitiveness and international connectivity. Partnership targets container capacity expansion The planned terminal will add significant container-handling capacity at Marunda Port. The development also marks another step in Gulftainer’s expansion across Southeast Asia. In September 2026, the company announced a strategic investment in Suksawat Terminal in Thailand. That agreement established its entry into the Thai market and formed part of its wider international expansion strategy. The latest partnership extends Gulftainer’s regional development activities to Indonesia, working alongside MSC’s Terminal Investment Limited and KCN. However, the companies have not yet disclosed the project’s investment value, ownership structure or construction schedule. A target date for the start of terminal operations has also not been announced. Further details about the proposed facility and its development phases remain to be confirmed.

articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Operations Tankers Black Sea drone attacks trigger Romanian fighter jet scramble Sam Chambers November 16, 2026 0 121 1 minute read Three commercial vessels have been struck by drones near Romania’s Black Sea coast, prompting the scrambling of fighter jets and fresh warnings from Bucharest as the maritime war between Russia and Ukraine moves increasingly close to NATO territory. Romanian prime minister Luca Niculescu confirmed on Sunday that three ships had been attacked near the Sulina Canal, a vital shipping artery linking the Danube with the Black Sea and used extensively for Ukrainian exports The vessels identified in reports of the weekend attacks include the Greek-flagged product tanker Evia Petrol V, the St Kitts and Nevis-flagged bulk carrier Marsol and the product tanker Ali Najafov. Fires broke out aboard the affected ships, but crews managed to extinguish them. No casualties were reported. Separately, the Palau-flagged cargo ship Larissa 1 was reportedly struck on Friday evening near Sfântu Gheorghe, around 12 km from the Romanian coast, damaging one of its cargo cranes. The ship was reportedly heading towards Ukraine. Romania’s armed forces scrambled fighter aircraft on two occasions after detecting aerial threats near its territorial waters. “These incidents are unacceptable and constitute a violation of international law,” Niculescu said. Romanian authorities have not established the origin of the drones, although officials linked the incidents to the widening consequences of Russia’s war against Ukraine. Meanwhile, Ukraine has stepped up its campaign against Russian energy infrastructure. Over the weekend, Ukrainian forces struck the TAIF-NK refinery and neighbouring Nizhnekamskneftekhim petrochemical complex in Tatarstan, more than 1,000 km inside Russia, triggering fires at both facilities. Fresh satellite imagery published on Sunday also revealed the extent of damage from Ukraine’s November 11 attack on Russia’s Baltic export port of Ust-Luga. At least five petroleum storage tanks were burned out. The expanding maritime confrontation comes as European authorities intensify their crackdown on Russia’s shadow fleet. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas confirmed on Sunday that European naval forces had boarded the tanker Midag in the Mediterranean on Friday, establishing that it was sailing under a false flag. EU foreign ministers are due to consider further sanctions today targeting banks, buyers and companies supporting Russia’s shadow fleet. articles.title: Steering failure blamed for New Orleans tanker-cruise ship collision
articles.summary: A steering failure aboard the asphalt tanker Atlantic Asphalt has emerged as the likely cause of Friday’s collision with a river cruise ship in New Orleans, with US investigators revealing that the vessel lost steering control just two minutes before impact. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said...
articles.body: Americas Operations Tankers Steering failure blamed for New Orleans tanker-cruise ship collision Sam Chambers November 16, 2026 0 86 1 minute read US Coast Guard Heartland US Coast Guard Heartland A steering failure aboard the asphalt tanker Atlantic Asphalt has emerged as the likely cause of Friday’s collision with a river cruise ship in New Orleans, with US investigators revealing that the vessel lost steering control just two minutes before impact. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said preliminary analysis of the tanker’s voyage data recorder showed its rudder became stuck to starboard at approximately 12.26 pm local time on November 13, sending the vessel towards the eastern bank of the Mississippi River At 12.28 pm, the 17,764 dwt tanker struck American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage , which was berthed at the Port of New Orleans. Investigators have yet to establish what caused the steering malfunction. As the tanker veered towards the riverbank, bridge recordings captured sounds consistent with the ship’s whistle, radio warnings, requests for assistance, commands to deploy anchors and emergency shiphandling orders. NTSB investigator Bart Barnum said the circumstances surrounding the steering failure remained under close examination. “It could be many different things,” Barnum said. Investigators have recovered more than nine hours of data from the tanker’s voyage recorder, including bridge audio, rudder angles, engine performance, speed and course. The NTSB also revealed that American Heritage , which was carrying 140 passengers and 50 crew, capsized within just 22 minutes of the collision. Thirty-two people were hospitalised, including two police officers thrown into the river during the incident. Six remained in hospital on Sunday. No fatalities have been reported. Salvage preparations are underway, with authorities working to remove approximately 16,000 gallons of diesel from the stricken cruise vessel before attempting to raise it. The operation could take more than a month. The investigation is examining whether Atlantic Asphalt’s anchors were deployed and at what depth. Interviews with the tanker’s 19 crewmembers are scheduled throughout this week. Meanwhile, the tanker remains subject to a federal arrest warrant after the Port of New Orleans launched legal proceedings against its owner, Nave Shipping, and manager OSM Thome, seeking more than $1m in damages to the Thalia Street Terminal. The NTSB expects to publish its preliminary findings within 30 days, with a final investigation report potentially taking up to two years. articles.title: Readers Speak: Shipping lines and cargo owners share expectations for Suez return
articles.summary: The gradual return of container shipping services to the Suez Canal is raising questions about which parts of the supply chain stand to benefit most. In the latest Container News Readers Speak poll, shipping lines and cargo owners emerged as the two leading choices, with neither establishing a decisive advantage. The...
articles.body: The gradual return of container shipping services to the Suez Canal is raising questions about which parts of the supply chain stand to benefit most. In the latest Container News Readers Speak poll, shipping lines and cargo owners emerged as the two leading choices, with neither establishing a decisive advantage. The findings suggest that readers see the potential benefits of shorter shipping routes extending beyond vessel operators to the businesses that depend on reliable and efficient cargo transportation. Ports, terminals and freight forwarders attracted less support, highlighting where expectations are currently concentrated. Shipping lines and cargo owners lead expectations Cargo owners held a marginal advantage in the larger response group, while shipping lines received slightly stronger support in the smaller group. Taken together, the findings point to a closely balanced outlook between the two. For shipping lines, a gradual return to Suez could reduce sailing distances, improve fleet utilisation and create greater flexibility in vessel deployment. Services currently operating around the Cape of Good Hope require longer voyages, which can increase operating costs and tie up additional capacity. However, shorter routes do not necessarily translate into higher profitability. The release of vessel capacity could intensify competition and place downward pressure on freight rates, depending on how carriers manage their networks. Cargo owners could benefit from shorter delivery times, potentially lower transportation costs and improved inventory planning. Yet these advantages will depend on actual service performance, freight market developments and the stability of shipping schedules. The close result reflects the different ways in which both groups could benefit from the same operational changes. Ports and freight forwarders receive less support Ports and terminals attracted relatively limited support, despite the potential for changes in shipping routes to reshape cargo flows and transshipment activity. A wider return to Suez could influence the role of Mediterranean and European gateways, particularly where carriers adjust port calls and connecting services. However, the impact would not necessarily be uniform, with some ports potentially gaining traffic while others face changes to existing network arrangements. Freight forwarders also received a smaller share of support. Although shorter routes could create opportunities for improved delivery planning and customer service, forwarders will still need to manage changing schedules, pricing conditions and the possibility of further disruptions. The results do not indicate that these sectors will remain unaffected. Rather, readers appear to expect the most immediate benefits to be concentrated among shipping lines and cargo owners. A gradual return with wider market implications Recent developments have strengthened the prospect of more container services using the Suez Canal. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have announced the rerouting of their Gemini Cooperation IOS/ME1 service, while Evergreen has begun restoring selected passages through the waterway. These developments represent a gradual, service-specific transition rather than a complete return of container shipping networks to their previous routes. Security conditions remain a central consideration, while the commercial effects will depend on vessel deployment, schedule reliability and the ability of carriers to maintain efficient connections across their networks. How this fits into the broader Readers Speak trend Previous Readers Speak discussions have highlighted the importance of reliability, operational flexibility and uncertainty in container shipping. The latest findings add a commercial dimension to those concerns by focusing on how the benefits of changing routes may be distributed across the supply chain. The near balance between shipping lines and cargo owners suggests that readers do not view the Suez return exclusively as an operational advantage for carriers or a cost-saving opportunity for customers. Instead, the results point to two closely connected expectations: more efficient shipping networks and improved conditions for cargo transportation. Whether those expectations are realised will depend on how the gradual return develops and how effectively the industry manages the transition.
takeaways: The gradual return of container shipping services to the Suez Canal is raising questions about which parts of the supply chain stand to benefit most.

The findings suggest that readers see the potential benefits of shorter shipping routes extending beyond vessel operators to the businesses that depend on reliable and efficient cargo transportation.

articles.title: US extends Jones Act waiver into February
articles.summary: Washington has extended its Jones Act waiver for another 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged vessels to continue competing for selected domestic cargo movements between US ports into February next year. The Department of Homeland Security approved the third extension of the waiver introduced in March, according to a...
articles.body: Americas Containers Dry Cargo Operations Regulatory Tankers US extends Jones Act waiver into February Adis Ajdin November 16, 2026 0 2,765 1 minute read White House White House Washington has extended its Jones Act waiver for another 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged vessels to continue competing for selected domestic cargo movements between US ports into February next year. The Department of Homeland Security approved the third extension of the waiver introduced in March, according to a November 13 notice from US Customs and Border Protection. The new period starts on November 16. Eligible cargo must be loaded before 11.59 pm Eastern Time on February 14, 2027. Foreign-flagged ships will still need individual approval before undertaking coastwise voyages. Cargo interests must submit vessel availability requests to the relevant US authorities, after which the Maritime Administration will survey the market to determine whether suitable Jones Act-qualified tonnage is available. The requirement keeps the tighter approval system introduced in August rather than restoring the broader exemptions available earlier in the year. The waiver was initially introduced in March amid disruption to US fuel supplies and shipping markets following the outbreak of war with Iran. It allows specified commodities to move between domestic ports aboard vessels that would ordinarily be barred from the trade under the Jones Act. The latest extension has drawn renewed criticism from the American Maritime Partnership, which represents US maritime interests and wants the exemption brought to an end. The group urged Washington to continue scrutinising individual applications, warning against allowing foreign vessels to displace American ships and crews on routine commercial movements. The Jones Act generally reserves domestic waterborne cargo movements for US-built, US-owned and US-flagged vessels meeting the law’s requirements. The extension leaves those restrictions in place outside the approved waiver arrangements. articles.title: Hong Kong’s five-year clock
articles.summary: From tax reform and green bunkering to ship registration and a new partnership with Shanghai, the government in Hong Kong is pursuing an increasingly ambitious maritime strategy. The challenge is turning policy commitments into lasting commercial activity. The latest instalment from our new Hong Kong magazine, which...
articles.body: Greater China Hong Kong’s five-year clock Splash November 16, 2026 0 524 4 minutes read From tax reform and green bunkering to ship registration and a new partnership with Shanghai, the government in Hong Kong is pursuing an increasingly ambitious maritime strategy. The challenge is turning policy commitments into lasting commercial activity. The latest instalment from our new Hong Kong magazine, which is being distributed across the city’s maritime week. Hong Kong’s government is attempting something more ambitious than rescuing a declining container port. It wants to turn the territory into what it calls a “global maritime capital”, earning more from the financing, insuring, managing and fuelling of ships even if fewer containers cross its quays. That change in emphasis has gathered pace throughout 2026. February’s budget proposed fresh shipping incentives, June brought tax legislation, September produced Hong Kong’s first five-year development plan and October has already seen proposed regulatory changes for green bunkering and a new agreement with Shanghai. The latest move came on October 20, when transport and logistics secretary Mable Chan signed a “brother port” cooperation agreement with Shanghai. The two cities intend to coordinate liner services, intermodal logistics, green shipping and maritime professional services. The agreement is significant for a port that has struggled against mainland competition: Hong Kong’s strategy increasingly relies on partnership rather than attempting to regain its former position in the container rankings. The clearest statement of intent came in the 2026-2030 plan and chief executive John Lee’s September policy address. The administration has explicitly called for a transition from “volume to value”, setting targets to reduce emissions from Kwai Tsing’s container terminals by 30% from 2021 levels, establish five green energy corridors and have 7% of Hong Kong-registered ships take up green maritime fuels by 2030. Green bunkering offers the most visible evidence of policy being translated into operations. Hong Kong completed its first methanol bunkering operation in March, followed days later by methanol bunkering alongside container handling at Kwai Tsing. From June 16, vessels carrying, using or bunkering eligible alternative fuels became entitled to port dues reductions of 25% or 50%, while qualifying Hong Kong-registered green-fuel ships can claim HK$60,000 annually for three years. The budget earmarks HK$34m for the incentives. In October the government gazetted measures to expand sea room available for green-fuel bunkering from 645 hectares to 2,877 hectares, including seven new anchorages. This is the sort of unglamorous infrastructure reform that matters to owners and suppliers assessing whether vessels can bunker safely without upsetting schedules. Yet storage and supply remain unfinished business. The administration wants green-fuel storage facilities at Tsing Yi South, with planning procedures scheduled for 2027 and tenders in early 2028. It also intends to announce its first green energy corridor with a mainland city later this year, connecting Chinese fuel production with international shipping demand. A green-fuel trading platform and carbon-accounting framework are also being explored. “Owners will ultimately bunker where fuel is available safely, consistently and at a competitive delivered price,” says Vikrant Gusain, chief executive of Dockendale Group. It is a reminder that incentives cannot substitute for dependable physical supply. Finance + Shipping agenda A second strand involves attracting commercial activity ashore. A bill gazetted in June seeks to improve shipping-related tax concessions, including adjustments to accommodate international minimum-tax rules, and introduce half-rate profits tax for qualifying physical commodity traders. The legislation remains before lawmakers in October. The rationale is that commodity trading produces demand for chartering, insurance, finance and maritime legal services. Simply offering lower tax rates to shipowners will not, by itself, rebuild that ecosystem. Richard Hext, chairman of the Hong Kong Shipowners Association, welcomes the administration’s proposed ‘Finance + Shipping’ agenda, which seeks to join ship finance, marine insurance and arbitration into a more compelling package. The government wants more underwriting capacity for specialist marine risks and is supporting the Hong Kong Shipowners Mutual Assurance Association’s development of international business, alongside promotion of the city’s arbitration services. But Hext offers a useful measure of success. “The next phase should be judged by substantive functions, regional headquarters, underwriting authority, credit decisions, trading desks and skilled jobs, and not by company registrations alone,” he says. Ship registration is another target. The government is preparing legislation to permit dual registration arrangements for bareboat-chartered ships, allowing owners to suspend one registration temporarily while a vessel operates under another flag. The objective is to make Hong Kong’s registry more useful to the increasingly complicated leasing and chartering structures of international fleets. The changes remain proposals rather than enacted reforms. At the port At the waterfront, the Port Community System launched in January to connect cargo information across sea, land and air. By September, more than 8,000 enterprises had registered and verified cargo data had supported more than 20 successful trade-finance applications. The next stage promises offshore cargo tracking using blockchain technology, while Kwai Tsing is earmarked for greater use of remotely operated cranes, autonomous electric vehicles and shore power. The city is also seeking new inland cargo through expanded rail-sea and river-sea links and deeper cooperation with Greater Bay Area ports. More direct liner connections to Central and South America are among the government’s priorities. Talent Then there is talent. Lee has proposed a maritime academy built around cooperation between educational institutions and employers, and the five-year plan calls for closer engagement with mainland training institutions and maritime technology researchers. “If I could choose one thing, it would be accelerating our maritime talent strategy,” says Angad Banga, chief executive of The Caravel Group. “Talent takes far longer to develop.” Promotion is part of the offensive too. The tenth Hong Kong Maritime Week takes place in November, with the government, shipowners and the International Chamber of Shipping bringing international executives together in the territory. The strategy is wide-ranging, but the industry still sees gaps in execution and governance. Horace Lo, group managing director of Modern Terminals, identifies “the establishment of a Maritime and Port Authority, and closer collaboration among ports in the GBA” as priorities. Others want faster progress on physical fuel storage and greater evidence that financing and insurance decisions are actually being made locally. Hong Kong now has a more detailed maritime programme than it has had for years. Its credibility will depend not on how many initiatives are announced, but on whether they bring cargo, capital, specialist jobs and commercial authority back to the city. articles.title: Norway’s court invalidates approvals for three offshore developments
articles.summary: Norway’s Supreme Court has ruled that government approvals for three major North Sea oil and gas developments are invalid because their environmental assessments failed to adequately account for greenhouse gas emissions. The ruling concerns Equinor’s Breidablikk field and Aker BP’s Tyrving and Yggdrasil developments,...
articles.body: Europe Offshore Norway’s court invalidates approvals for three offshore developments Bojan Lepic November 16, 2026 0 129 1 minute read Equinor Equinor Norway’s Supreme Court has ruled that government approvals for three major North Sea oil and gas developments are invalid because their environmental assessments failed to adequately account for greenhouse gas emissions. The ruling concerns Equinor’s Breidablikk field and Aker BP’s Tyrving and Yggdrasil developments, whose approval processes environmental organisations Greenpeace and Natur og Ungdom challenged in 2023. All 11 Supreme Court judges agreed that environmental assessments must examine emissions resulting from the eventual combustion of oil and gas, including their contribution to global warming. However, the court was split six to five on whether those assessments must also consider cumulative emissions from existing and approved developments across the Norwegian continental shelf. The majority concluded that the government’s assessments were insufficient and declared the development approvals invalid on procedural grounds. The judgment does not automatically revoke the companies’ permits or require production to stop, as the operators were not parties to the proceedings. Norway’s Ministry of Energy must now reconsider the approvals under the correct environmental assessment requirements. Energy minister Terje Aasland said the government would address the shortcomings as quickly as possible, but did not expect the ruling to disrupt existing production or development activities. Breidablikk began producing in October 2023, followed by Tyrving in September 2024. Production from the much larger Yggdrasil development is scheduled to begin in 2027. The ruling could also affect future offshore project approvals by introducing more extensive climate assessment requirements. articles.body: Americas Europe Offshore Subsea 7 lands US Gulf deepwater contract Bojan Lepic November 16, 2026 0 75 1 minute read Subsea 7 Subsea 7 Norwegian offshore engineering and construction specialist Subsea 7 has secured a contract worth between $50m and $150m from Kosmos Energy for the Tiberius development in the US Gulf. The deal covers the fabrication, transportation and installation of a 14 km steel catenary riser and wet-insulated flowline connecting the deepwater development to Occidental’s existing Lucius spar. Subsea 7 will also install an umbilical and subsea control systems at the project, located in Keathley Canyon block 964, at a depth of approximately 2,200 m. Engineering and project management will begin in the coming months at the company’s Houston office, with offshore installation scheduled to start in 2028. Tiberius was discovered in 2023, with the partners taking a final investment decision on the initial development phase in March this year. The first phase involves completing an existing well and tying it back to Lucius, with first oil targeted for the second half of 2028. Initial production capacity is estimated at around 13,000 barrels per day. Subsequent development phases could include additional wells, potentially increasing production to 30,000 barrels of oil and 9m cubic feet of gas per day. Earlier this year, Eni and NOC commissioned a separate compression project at Sabratha, adding approximately 440m cubic feet per day of compression capacity to help sustain production from the mature field. REUTERS/Christiana Botic By Siddharth Cavale Nov 15 (Reuters) – The asphalt tanker vessel that struck a docked paddlewheel cruise boat in the Mississippi River at New Orleans last week experienced a steering problem in which its rudder was stuck in one position, US transportation safety officials said on Sunday. The American ?Cruise Lines paddlewheeler American Heritage, with 190 people aboard, capsized at the dock. No one was killed in the collision on Friday. The Atlantic Asphalt tanker was headed upriver when it experienced a “steering casualty” in which its rudder stayed in a starboard position and the vessel veered toward the river’s east bank, National Transportation Safety Board senior marine accident investigator Bart Barnum told a news conference in New Orleans. NTSB officials said they do not know what caused the steering problem. The tanker’s voyage-data recorder was recovered on Saturday. Investigators downloaded more than nine hours of data and began analyzing information that includes bridge audio, rudder angle, propulsion performance and vessel speed, Barnum said. Recorder data showed the asphalt tanker was traveling upriver on Friday near the Crescent City Connection Bridge at about 12:26 p.m. local time (1826 GMT), two minutes before the collision, when it experienced the steering issue, Barnum said. The cruise ship capsized in about 22 minutes, NTSB officials said on Sunday. As the American Heritage toppled over into the river after the impact, harbor personnel, firefighters and onlookers scrambled to pull passengers to safety. Interviews with the crew of the Atlantic Asphalt are scheduled over the next week, NTSB officials said. The agency will release a preliminary report in about 30 days, the agency said. articles.title: Tankers: A Crude Correction, But Rates Remain Well Above Historical Levels
articles.summary: A combination of factors have forced the tanker market rates lower this past month, but they still remain quite elevated by historical standards. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Gibson said that “crude tanker freight rates have taken a beating this month albeit from unprecedented highs, with key benchmarks...
articles.body: Tankers: A Crude Correction, But Rates Remain Well Above Historical Levels in Hellenic Shipping News 16/11/2026 A combination of factors have forced the tanker market rates lower this past month, but they still remain quite elevated by historical standards. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Gibson said that “crude tanker freight rates have taken a beating this month albeit from unprecedented highs, with key benchmarks dropping more than 50%. The rout started following the Democratic wins in the midterm elections, whilst a more de-escalatory tone from President Trump shifted sentiment in financial and commodity markets. Given the surge in freight rates seen this year was not driven purely by quantifiable factors, it is easy to blame sentiment for the fall in tanker rates. Undoubtedly this was a major factor, but it is not the only influence driving rates lower”. According to Gibson, “in terms of risk premiums, the immediate danger involved in a Hormuz transit remains unchanged. However, paper markets are less fearful of the future. In the physical markets, refiners are less concerned about oil supply than they were a few months ago. Indeed, a recent JPMorgan reported pointed to a surplus of 1.1mbd in September, rising to 1.4mbd last month, alleviating the need to panic buy. The IEA placed the October surplus higher at 1.7mbd with softer demand also contributing to the stock build”. “Supply chains have also been adapting to the current status quo. Since Saudi Arabia’s East–West pipeline resumed flows in September, the market has kept a relatively steady trade pattern. This has allowed tanker positioning to adjust, with vessels increasingly repositioning East to capture higher Hormuz volumes. In recent weeks VLCC supply in the Middle East has risen sharply, prompting sharp corrections on Gulf of Oman freight rates. Suezmaxes and Aframaxes in the West have also seen very sharp corrections. Extremely elevated freight levels inevitably dampened cargo enquiry and prompted Europe to increase its intake of Saudi barrels from Sidi Kerir in recent weeks, at the expense of longer-haul trades, which ultimately increased tonnage availability”, the shipbroker added. Source: Gibson Shipbrokers Ltd Meanwhile, Gibson also noted that “the poor weather which helped boost inefficiencies for midsize tankers in October has subsided, whilst cargo volumes have started the month lower. Aframaxes have been impacted by rising supply, with over 115 vessels joining the fleet this year, either through LR2s switching to dirty or newbuildings being delivered. Suezmaxes have had 43 new deliveries for the year to date. 35 new VLCCs have joined the fleet while an ever-increasing number of older vessels with questionable trading history have joined the Hormuz shuttle fleet. As such vessel availability has improved almost everywhere with more coming”. “Falling crude prices further weighed on tanker rates. Though the two are not always correlated, with freight being such a high share of cargo value, falling flat prices have forced freight to adjust to keep trades workable. Earlier this year, it was often commodity prices which had to adjust to keep arbs open, now increasingly freight is doing the work. Ultimately refining margins were being squeezed, consumer demand was under pressure from high pump prices. As such, freight rates were unsustainably high. Something had to give”, the shipbroker noted. “However, looking ahead it is important to note that risk is still high, Iranian oil has all but disappeared from the market, Chinese imports have recovered to the highest level since March, flows through Hormuz remain robust (though under threat from persistent attacks), operational inefficiencies are high and global oil inventories need rebuilding. Lower freight rates will reopen trading opportunities, and the risk of renewed conflict cannot be worn out. Bad weather often drives volatility in Q4 and Q1. Most importantly, even after this month’s correction, freight rates and earnings in the crude sector remain exceptionally strong by historic standards and with no end in sight to the wars in the Gulf and Ukraine, geopolitics will continue to call the shots”, Gibson concluded. articles.title: IMO faces challenges in net-zero framework compliance without emissions cost
articles.summary: Countries are struggling to design rules to make shipping companies comply with a new bunker regulation designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, a senior International Bunker Industry Association official said Nov. 12, as Washington leads opposition to financial punitive measures. International Maritime...
articles.body: IMO faces challenges in net-zero framework compliance without emissions cost in International Shipping News 16/11/2026 Countries are struggling to design rules to make shipping companies comply with a new bunker regulation designed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, a senior International Bunker Industry Association official said Nov. 12, as Washington leads opposition to financial punitive measures. International Maritime Organization member states, having failed to adopt the Net-Zero Framework as scheduled in October 2025, are due to meet again between Nov. 23 and Dec. 4 to discuss the regulation. “People recognize that we need a GHG intensity marine fuel standard, and that is sort of generally agreed,” Edmund Hughes, IBIA’s representative to the UN agency, told Platts. “The sticking point is on the financial aspects.” In its current form, the framework is composed of GHG intensity thresholds for marine energy that tighten progressively over 2028-2035, and financial costs for shipping companies failing to meet the standards. But the US has fiercely opposed what it describes as “a global carbon tax” on shipping for the financial element, and a growing number of member states have proposed various revisions to the framework in bids to achieve a compromise. “That is where we have the trouble. Because, obviously, the member states haven’t been able to identify the best approach,” Hughes said on the sidelines of the IBIA Annual Convention 2026. Compliance mechanism Countries supporting the current net-zero framework have designed the financial element to promote the use of low-carbon marine fuels, which remain much more costly than conventional, oil-based fuels due to limited availability. October’s average delivered bunker costs for 0.5%-sulfur fuel oil are $22.78 per gigajoule in Singapore, compared with $27/GJ for bioblend B24, $28.48/GJ for LNG, and $48.47/GJ for 100% sustainable methanol, according to the Platts global bunker cost calculator. “No shipping company is going to carry on buying more expensive fuel while their competitors are not,” Hughes said. “You need some way of closing that price gap.” The IBIA official said challenges lie ahead for member states on how to design an alternative compliance mechanism if the current net-zero framework is to be revised. Most Pacific Island states and EU member states are officially still supporting the current net-zero framework while the US and Middle Eastern states remain opposed to it. Japan, China, Norway and some major flag states have presented new ideas on compliance mechanisms. “If you have a technical standard, you have to find a way to comply with it,” Hughes said. “You can go through quite a few semantic gymnastics to try and get the agreement, and that’s often what’s done at international level in multilateral discussions.” Outlook IBIA, the world’s largest trade association representing bunker industry participants, including bunker traders and fuel suppliers, has been granted consultative status with the IMO and its representatives regularly participate in IMO meetings. “We recognize and value, as a sector, having global rules,” Hughes said. “That helps in all sorts of aspects in terms of understanding what the compliance requirements are, understanding what the market needs, what we need to provide in terms of fuels, and what people want to buy.” Going forward, Hughes said IMO member states may need to coalesce around a net-zero framework in a return to its tradition of consensus building so future implementation could be ensured globally. In April 2025, a total of 63 countries won a vote to approve the framework’s current text after the US withdrew from the negotiations. Later, 57 countries won another vote to delay its adoption in October 2025. “There was a vote… that already sent a clear signal that there was no consensus,” Hughes said. “The people who win a vote might think they won, but they [actually] lost.” Source: Platts 2026-11-16 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: Dry Bulk Shipping: Capesizes Retain Positive Momentum in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 16/11/2026 C apesize The Capesize market maintained a positive trajectory throughout the week, with the Pacific emerging as the clear driver of overall gains. Despite some midweek volatility, improving miner demand and increasingly competitive fixing levels saw C5 recover strongly, climbing from $13.80 on Monday to $15.20 by Thursday, before easing back to $14.50–$14.60 towards the end of the week. Activity picked up considerably, particularly from Wednesday onwards, with both Port Hedland and Dampier miners covering multiple cargoes and operators increasingly willing to pay into the low-mid $15s. The Atlantic presented a more mixed picture. North Atlantic sentiment remained positive, supported by improving demand on the Transatlantic and Fronthaul routes, while the South Brazil and West Africa to China markets struggled to establish similar momentum. C3 levels softened as the week progressed, with fixtures slipping from around $36 to $35, reflecting limited index-date demand and a widening gap between bids and offers. Overall, the BCI 182 5TC built on its $40,000 level, reaching a high of $43,860 before closing the week at $42,798. Pacific strength and North Atlantic resilience ultimately outweighed continued pressure in the South Atlantic. Panamax-Kamsarmax The market delivered contrasting performances this week, with the Atlantic maintaining a firm tone while the Pacific struggled to gain momentum. Strong transatlantic demand and limited prompt tonnage supported rates, with an 82,000-dwt fixing around $18,000 for a US East Coast round trip and another at $22,250 basis South Africa for an East Coast South America transatlantic trip. Increasing North Continent tonnage availability offered charterers greater flexibility, while an 82,000-dwt secured $27,350 for a US Gulf fronthaul to China. East Coast South America remained supported by tighter early December tonnage, with an 83,000-dwt fixing at $18,750 plus $875,000 ballast bonus to the Far East and an 81,000-dwt at $18,500 basis retroactive East Coast India delivery. Meanwhile, growing Pacific tonnage availability outweighed Australian mineral demand, with an 82,000-dwt fixing at $22,500 early in the week compared with a 77,000-dwt at $19,000 towards the close. North Pacific and Indonesian activity remained subdued, with an 82,000-dwt fixing at $19,500 and a 76,000-dwt at $17,000 respectively. Period activity included an 83,000-dwt fixing five to seven months at $17,000 and an 81,000-dwt for one year at $18,000, both basis Pacific delivery. Ultramax/Supramax After declining for two weeks, the 11TC average showed positive returns in the second half of the week due to an improving Atlantic market. The North American market saw extremely limited tonnage for November dates, with transatlantic rates flying to new highs as a 63,000-dwt fixed for grains US Gulf to Continent/Mediterranean at $39,000 and a 64,000-dwt fixed for similar business at $40,000. A 61,000-dwt fixed petcoke to the East Mediterranean at $42,000, and a 64,000-dwt was said to have fixed on voyage on the same route in the mid $40,000s. There were modest gains in the South Atlantic, whilst the Continent and Mediterranean markets remained steady in light trading. Rates slowly softened in Asia as NoPac grains slowed, with a 64,000-dwt fixed for a round voyage at $21,000 and a 63,000-dwt concluded at $27,000 basis North China via NoPac to Bangladesh, whilst backhaul demand remained strong. Further south, the market was affected by a weak Indian Ocean market with ballasting tonnage competing for Indonesian stems, with larger units switching attention to Australian cargoes for better returns. With a falling spot market in the East, there was limited period activity, however a modern 63,000-dwt still managed to fix a strong $24,500 for 6 to 8 months basis delivery CJK. Handysize The week completed on a steady-to-firmer note, with sentiment largely positional across both basins. Across the Continent and Mediterranean, activity remained limited, although rates began to show signs of firmness towards the end of the week. The 37,000-dwt open Italy fixed for a trip to South Africa with charterers’ option WC India at low $20,000. The US Gulf and South Atlantic showed healthier momentum, supported by fresh demand and a balanced cargo-to-tonnage position, with a number of fixtures reported, particularly from the US Gulf. A 39,000-dwt open Mobile fixed for a trip to UK with pellets at $23,000, while a 37,000-dwt open Santos fixed via Brazil to Singapore–Japan range with parcels at $24,000. Across Asia, sentiment remained positive, with activity gaining pace and several fixtures concluded above previous levels, supported by a generally healthy balance between tonnage availability and cargo demand. articles.summary: VLCC supply is starting to arrive. After a sharp rise in ordering, the first of the new tonnage is reaching the water, with deliveries already well ahead of last year. articles.body: VLCC Deliveries Rise Fivefold as the Orderbook Builds in International Shipping News 16/11/2026 V LCC supply is starting to arrive. After a sharp rise in ordering, the first of the new tonnage is reaching the water, with deliveries already well ahead of last year. Using VesselsValue data, we look at what is on order, who is building it, and why owners keep ordering at near-record prices. VLCC deliveries have moved significantly higher. There were just seven VLCCs delivered across the whole of 2025, while 35 have already delivered this year, five times the 2025 total. The pipeline behind them is substantial, with 349 VLCCs on order or launched, and the delivery schedule is heavily weighted to the next few years, with 125 due in 2028 and 113 in 2029. Overall, 27.3% of the VLCC fleet is on order. China sits at the centre of VLCC deliveries China holds 268 of the VLCCs on order, c.77% of the orderbook, and builds 106 of the 125 units, due in 2028. South Korea accounts for 59 and Japan for 15, so the build programme is firmly concentrated in one country. Our recent market chat on new and established yards entering the Tanker market looks at how this capacity is being added. Notable recent orders include three 320,000 DWT VLCCs ordered by Bahri, set to be built at International Maritime Industries (IMI) and set for delivery in 2029, contracted at USD 150.3 mil each en bloc, VV Value USD 127.69 mil. IMI is Saudi Arabia’s first large-scale shipbuilding project, and these are the only VLCCs on order at a Saudi yard. 219 VLCCs have been ordered this year to date, compared to just 85 in 2025, and newbuilding values have risen with it. Prices are up 15% year-on-year, from USD 125.59 mil to USD 144.51 mil, close to the all-time high of USD 154 mil in Oct 2008. Why demand is holding up despite high prices and a large orderbook Replacement alone does not explain it, as the 349 VLCCs on order or launched compares with 183 vessels aged 20 years and above. Tankers have been in short supply in recent years because of sanctions and geopolitics, and the situation in the Strait of Hormuz has tightened availability further. Earnings have reached levels that were previously unthinkable, which strengthens the case for newbuilding even at current prices. Middle Eastern producers are also a factor. With shipowners reluctant to transit the Strait of Hormuz since the disruption began, some producers have looked to buy or build their own VLCCs so that they have vessels available to move their crude whatever the conditions. This moves them from relying on the open market for tonnage to owning the capacity they need to get barrels out, and it adds a further source of newbuilding demand alongside strong earnings. The age profile shows where supply could be removed if conditions change. Of the 932 VLCCs in the fleet, 45.8% are 15 years or older, including 183 vessels aged 20 years and above. That leaves a sizeable pool of tonnage that could be considered for demolition should the market weaken. VLCC deliveries continue to build Taken together, the data points to a VLCC fleet that is about to grow at a pace not seen in recent years, with the build programme concentrated in China and delivery volumes weighted to 2028 and 2029. Demand for newbuildings has held up so far because earnings, tight tonnage availability, and energy security concerns have outweighed the cost of ordering at near-record prices. Should conditions change, the ageing fleet offers a sizeable pool of tonnage that could leave the market, so the balance between deliveries and demolition will be one to watch. Signal Ocean’s tracked flows show Australian bauxite exports reached 51.44 Mt during January–October 2026, down 4.8% from 54.05 Mt a year earlier and slightly below the 51.73 Mt recorded in the same period of 2024. The decline was not uniform throughout the year. Q3 shipments increased 6.4% quarter-on-quarter to 17.08 Mt, although they remained 5.1% below the corresponding period of 2025. October exports reached 5.79 Mt, down 3.2% month-on-month but 1.3% higher year-on-year. China’s share of Australian bauxite exports has grown. Australian bauxite shipments to China increased 2.7% year-over-year to 36.41 Mt during January–October 2026, while exports to other destinations declined 19.1% to 15.03 Mt. China’s share of Australia’s total bauxite exports rose to 70.8%, up from 65.6% a year earlier. The divergence was more pronounced in October, when China-bound shipments increased 13.6% year-over-year to 4.37 Mt, while volumes to other destinations fell 23.9%. A softer start to November. Signal Ocean’s tracked Australian bauxite exports declined to 0.88 Mt in the week ending 8 November, down 28.7% week-on-week and 31.8% year-on-year. China-bound shipments eased 10.6% on the week to 0.75 Mt, while exports to other destinations fell more sharply, by 67.3%, to 0.13 Mt. The latest weekly decline was therefore more pronounced outside China, consistent with the growing concentration of Australian bauxite shipments towards the Chinese market. However, the weekly figures should be viewed alongside October’s 1.3% year-on-year increase in total exports. Australian supply and Chinese demand. Metro Mining reported improved shipments from its Bauxite Hills operation, with October exports reaching 752,000 wet tonnes, approximately 14% above September, following earlier mining and barging disruptions. Loading performance also improved, with a Capesize vessel loaded in 5.8 days, the company’s fastest turnaround of 2026. In China, aluminium ingot inventories across three major regions declined by 6,000 t to 370,000 t on 11 November. However, conditions further upstream remain less supportive of additional bauxite purchases. Weekly Chinese alumina production fell to 1.733 Mt as of 5 November, with the operating rate declining to 75.55%. Improved Australian loading capacity may therefore not immediately translate into stronger spot cargo demand. China’s increasing share of Australian bauxite exports favours shorter Pacific voyages over the longer Guinea–China route, with different implications for Capesize tonne-mile demand. articles.body: The Week in Alt Fuels: A drop in the tank in International Shipping News 16/11/2026 Several producers are developing small-scale low- and zero-emission fuel projects around the world. But shipping needs far greater volumes available at competitive prices and at major bunker locations. Several small-scale biofuel and e-fuel projects are being developed around the world. Swiss startup Synhelion expects to start commercial operations at its 1,000 mt/year synthetic fuel plant in Germany in 2028. German-Brazilian startup Atlanteo is developing a modular e-methanol production concept, with its first 20 MW plant expected to produce around 10,000 mt/year. European Energy’s Kassø e-methanol facility in Aabenraa, Denmark, which is already operating, produced 4,974 mt of e-methanol in the first half of 2026, against a planned capacity of 32,000 mt/year. The company is also planning a 48,000 mt/year e-methanol plant in Québec, Canada, with Greenfield Global. ENGIE is planning a biomethane production facility at the HAROPA port complex in France, with an expected output of 7,000 mt/year intended for CMA CGM’s LNG-capable fleet. Smaller-capacity projects can help developers test technologies, identify production challenges and establish commercial supply chains. But proving a concept works is one thing. Making it work at scale to meet potential demand is another. A large ocean-going vessel can consume thousands of mt/year of fuel. That puts the output of a 1,000 mt/year plant into perspective. Even a 10,000 mt/year facility could typically serve only a limited number of vessels, depending on their size and fuel consumption. And shipping is hardly the only customer waiting at the door. A number of low- and zero-emission fuel producers are diversifying the allocations across multiple sectors, including aviation, road transport, chemicals and fertilisers, leaving several industries competing for the same molecules. Then comes the cost of getting that fuel to ships. Producing renewable fuel at a competitive price doesn’t automatically make it a viable marine fuel option. Transport, storage and physical delivery costs can push up the final bunker price, particularly when production facilities are located far from major bunkering ports. Longer transport distances could also increase associated emissions, potentially reducing the environmental benefits of switching to cleaner fuels. This is where the distinction between scaling production and scaling supply becomes important. Some developers intend to expand existing facilities, while others are pursuing networks of smaller plants. Atlanteo, for instance, plans to replicate its modular facilities in locations with suitable renewable energy and agricultural resources. Synhelion has outlined plans for larger plants in Germany and Morocco. Both approaches could increase production capacity. But the real commercial test is whether that fuel can reach ocean-going vessels in sufficient quantities without logistics costs undermining its appeal. None of this diminishes the importance of smaller projects. They provide an opportunity to test technologies and work through practical challenges before committing to larger investments. But a successful pilot is only the beginning. For renewable fuels to make a meaningful contribution to deep-sea shipping, producers must eventually develop supply chains capable of delivering sufficient volumes at workable prices to the ports where vessels actually bunker. In other alt fuels news this week, Frontier Fuels has chartered a barge for B100 deliveries on the Elbe, for supplying ships at five ports, including Hamburg and Cuxhaven. The barge, Lina, will carry only B100 (100% biofuel), the company said. It will also deliver to ships in Stade, Kiel and Brunsbüttel. The VO Chidambaranar (VOC) Port Authority will commence methanol bunkering at the port by the end of November. The port’s methanol bunker infrastructure comprises an onshore storage facility connected to a jetty through a 2.8-km pipeline for shore-to-ship fuel transfers. US LNG bunker supplier REV LNG completed an LNG bunkering operation for Siem Car Carriers’ vessel Aristotle, marking the first such operation at the Port of Davisville in Rhode Island. The truck-to-ship operation also marks the first LNG fuelling of a car carrier in the US Northeast, according to REV LNG. PowerCell will supply fuel cells for an ammonia power project in Norway. The system is designed to generate 700 kW of electricity for commercial ships and will be tested in Stord ahead of commissioning in early 2028. Rates to Laem Chabang declined 6% to $1,557 per 40ft container, while those to Kaohsiung fell 3% to $1,297 per 40ft container. articles.body: Shandong Marine Corporation (SMC) has launched a new container shipping service connecting Rizhao in China’s Shandong Province with Incheon in South Korea, strengthening maritime links between the two countries. The port authority estimates that the route could generate approximately 120,000 TEU in additional annual container traffic. Rizhao is a major Chinese port serving industries including steel, petrochemicals and paper manufacturing. The new service adds another direct connection to Incheon’s existing container network with Shandong Province, which already includes Qingdao, Weihai, Yantai and Shidao. The introduction of RIX expands the range of regular maritime connections available to shippers moving cargo between eastern China and South Korea.

Last month, combined imports at the Port of Los Angeles and the Port of Long Beach came in at 1,000,500 TEUs, or 20-foot equivalent units, just off September’s all-time high. Compared to October last year, loaded import, export, and empty container volumes were up more than 20% at the Port of LA and more than 11% at the Port of Long Beach, according to data provided by the ports. Port of LA Executive Director Gene Seroka on Thursday attributed the sustained surge to changing trade policy and uncertainty along other global shipping routes, US consumer spending and retailers restocking inventory. Port of Long Beach CEO Noel Hacegaba said he expected elevated container volumes to continue through at least the beginning of next year as importers frontload goods before a US-China trade truce expires again in January. “We expect to be busy at least through the first month of the new year and possibly through the first quarter,” Hacegaba told Bloomberg last week, adding that cargo needed to supply the AI boom is among the growth drivers. Empty containers moving through both ports were 26% and 13% higher, a sign that ocean carriers were repositioning equipment for more shipments coming from Asia. The import surge across several of the busiest US ports is expected to taper off through the end of the year before falling 3% in January compared to the year before, according to the National Retail Federation. “Numbers are still strong even as the season winds down,” said Jonathan Gold, NRF’s VP for supply chain and customs policy. Gold noted in a statement earlier this week that the high volumes have led to backups, especially for rail-bound cargo at the major West Coast ports. Gold also warned of potential disruption to operations at the Ports of LA and Long Beach if a union of security workers and their employers don’t come to an agreement before a Nov. 20 deadline. Romanian Interior Ministry/Handout via REUTERS BUCHAREST, Nov 15 (Reuters) – Drones have struck three commercial ships in the Black Sea near Romania’s Sulina canal , Prime Minister Luca Niculescu said on Sunday, adding that his armed forces had scrambled fighter jets twice. Defence Minister Stefan Radu Oprea said there were no casualties and that the ships’ crews had managed to control the fires on board after the strikes late on Saturday. A growing series of deadly strikes on merchant ships near NATO members Romania and Bulgaria shows how the escalating maritime war between Russia and Ukraine is expanding into a major challenge for the transatlantic alliance in the Black Sea. The Sulina canal is a key Romanian shipping lane which links the Danube river to the Black Sea and is used by Ukraine for exports. Romanian officials did not identify the origin of the drones but said they were a direct consequence of Russia’s war in Ukraine . “These incidents are unacceptable and constitute a violation of international law,” Niculescu said. “They reflect the deteriorating security situation caused by Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.” Related Article: IMO Warns of Mounting Human Toll as Attacks on Commercial Shipping Continue Russia has denied targeting Ukraine’s neighbours with drones. Oprea said the three struck ships were Greek-flagged oil and chemical tanker Evia Petrol V, bulk carrier Marsol and oil products tanker Ali Najafov, both under the flag of Saint Kitts and Nevis. Evia Petrol V and Marsol were struck 4 and 5 nautical miles southeast of the Sulina canal, the defence ministry said, inside Romanian territorial waters. Oprea said a separate general cargo ship was hit by a drone late on Friday, also with no casualties. Private television station Digi24 said the vessel was Palau-flagged general cargo ship Larissa 1. “On Tuesday and Wednesday I will be in Brussels for the meeting with my fellow (defence) ministers,” Oprea said. “We need the solidarity of our allies, shown through patrols with surveillance aircraft and through equipment for counter-drone warfare.” France temporarily relocated the Atlantique 2 maritime patrols aircraft to Romania after it asked for reinforcement. articles.title: American Heritage Captain, Crew and Tug Operators Hailed as Heroes After Mississippi River Capsizing
articles.summary: The captain and crew of the American Heritage, along with tugboat operators and first responders who rushed to the scene, are being hailed as heroes following Friday’s dramatic collision on...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo credit: Tow Boaters Facebook group The captain and crew of the American Heritage , along with tugboat operators and first responders who rushed to the scene, are being hailed as heroes following Friday’s dramatic collision on the Mississippi River that left the river cruise ship capsized but everyone aboard alive. American Cruise Lines singled out Captain Leonard Stewart, who remained on the bridge as the vessel overturned after being struck by the tanker Atlantic Asphalt at the Port of New Orleans on November 13. “The fast actions of Captain Leonard Stewart and our crew allowed for a rapid evacuation of the vessel,” the company said in a statement Saturday. “Captain Stewart remained on the bridge as the vessel capsized, calling for aid and keeping the ship alongside the dock for as long as possible.” The collision occurred at approximately 12:30 p.m. local time, just below the Crescent City Connection bridge. The impact caused the American Heritage to take on water and eventually roll onto its side, sending passengers and crew into the Mississippi River. As the riverboat began to capsize, help arrived from nearly every direction. Harbor tugs, towboats and other working vessels raced toward the scene, joining the U.S. Coast Guard, Port of New Orleans Harbor Police, New Orleans Fire Department and other emergency responders in a massive rescue operation. AIS data and local reports showed crews from Moran Towing, Crescent Towing, Cooper Mooring, John W. Stone Oil Distributor and Canal Barge Co. responding within minutes of the collision. Among the vessels identified near the scene were Moran’s Becky S , Crescent Towing’s Mardi Gras and G. Shelby Friedrichs , the E.N. Bisso tug Marauder , and several Stone Oil towboats, including Presager , Madison Stone , Stephanie Stone and Stone Power . Canal Barge’s Elly Lane was also among the vessels identified, along with the Port of New Orleans fireboat Gen. Roy S. Kelley . While AIS positions alone do not establish the specific actions taken by every vessel, footage and accounts from the scene show working boats joining emergency craft in the rescue effort. Captain Kenny Brown of The Maritime Throwdown praised the private-sector crews whose contributions can sometimes be overlooked amid the attention given to government emergency responders. “When something goes wrong on the river, the first boats you usually see on scene are towboats and tugs,” Brown wrote. “Nobody calls them in. They’re already there, and they turn toward the trouble.” Brown credited the captains, pilots and deckhands who maneuvered their vessels into position and helped with the response. “To the captains who made the call, the pilots who held those boats steady, and the deckhands out on the deck with life rings and pike poles in hand: that’s courage, and the river saw it.” The response was extraordinary in its speed and scale. New Orleans Harbor Police Chief Melanie Montroll said 87 passengers and crew members were able to disembark before the American Heritage capsized. It then took approximately 30 to 45 minutes for rescuers to pull the remaining people from the river and account for everyone. Mayor Helena Moreno described the outcome as a “miracle on the Mississippi,” crediting the coordinated efforts of government responders and nearby vessels that voluntarily joined the rescue. All passengers and crew were accounted for, with no fatalities. Thirty-two people, including two Harbor Police officers, were transported to hospitals. Eight remained hospitalized as of Saturday, according to local officials. American Cruise Lines thanked the Coast Guard, Port of New Orleans, New Orleans Police Department and other agencies involved in the response. “We are proud of our crew and grateful for the first responders,” the company said, adding that it would continue cooperating with authorities through the investigation and salvage effort. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the collision, including reports that the Atlantic Asphalt may have experienced a steering failure before striking the docked riverboat. The cause has not been determined. The American Heritage remains partially submerged alongside the riverfront, with salvage operations expected to take weeks. For Brown, the incident also underscored the importance of maritime safety training, emergency drills and the ability to respond instinctively when seconds matter. “Practice until it’s muscle memory,” he wrote. “You don’t rise to the occasion. You fall back on your training.” The outcome in New Orleans was a reminder of the professionalism found across the maritime industry, from passenger vessel crews to the working mariners aboard the tugs and towboats that keep the Mississippi River moving. articles.body: CMA CGM has announced new Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) covering shipments from the Far East to South Africa and from Europe and the Mediterranean to Latin America and the Caribbean, with implementation dates in November and December 2026. The French container shipping company will introduce a surcharge of US$650 per TEU on shipments from the Far East to South Africa, effective from 15 November 2026. The measure applies to all cargo types and will remain in place until further notice. The surcharge will be determined by the loading date and covers cargo originating from Far East ports and destined for South Africa. New surcharges from Europe and Mediterranean to the Americas In a separate announcement, CMA CGM confirmed additional Peak Season Surcharges (PSS 02) on shipments from Northern Europe, the Mediterranean, North Africa and the Black Sea to destinations across Latin America and the Caribbean. The new charges will take effect on 7 December 2026, based on the loading date, and will remain applicable until further notice. All three measures apply exclusively to short-term contracts and cover all cargo types. For shipments originating in Northern Europe, excluding Portugal, and destined for the west coast of South America, the carrier will apply a surcharge of €200 per unit. A surcharge of €200 per unit will also apply to shipments originating from Mediterranean ports in Spain, Italy and France, as well as the Adriatic and Portugal. The measure covers destinations on the west coast of South America, the west coasts of Central America and Mexico, the east coast of Central America and the Caribbean, excluding the French West Indies. It also covers the Leeward Islands, excluding Gustavia and Philipsburg, and the Windward Islands. For shipments originating from the Eastern Mediterranean, Adriatic, North Africa and Black Sea, CMA CGM has announced a surcharge of US$200 per unit. This measure applies to the same destination regions, including the west coast of South America, the west coasts of Central America and Mexico, the east coast of Central America and the Caribbean, subject to the stated exclusions for the French West Indies, Gustavia and Philipsburg. The December surcharges will apply in addition to the carrier’s existing freight charges under the relevant contract terms. CMA CGM has not specified an expiry date for either announcement, with both measures remaining in effect until further notice.

REUTERS/Rogan Ward By Matthew Hill and Alexander Parker Nov 14, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Severe delays at South Africa’s biggest container terminal in the port city of Durban are threatening the nation’s auto industry, already under strain from a tide of cheap Asian imports and US tariffs. Dlouhy Nov 14, 2026 (Bloomberg) –President Donald Trump is giving energy companies and traders more time to transport oil and other commodities around the US on foreign-flagged ships, renewing a policy intended to lower fuel costs. Trump has decided to extend by 90 days a waiver of mandates under the century-old Jones Act that otherwise require cargo carried between US ports to be transported on American-owned, -flagged and -operated vessels, according to a White House official speaking on condition of anonymity before the decision is public. The extension comes just two days before a previous waiver was set to expire. It will take effect at 12 a.m. Monday New York time, ensuring no gap between the expiration of the prior one, the official said. The decision underscores the administration’s continued concerns about high energy costs due to the war in Iran , after Democrats trounced Republicans in the November midterm elections that were dominated by voter concerns about the cost of living. Trump did not change the breadth of the relief, after previously narrowing the waiver’s scope in August to require the government conduct case-by-case reviews of vessel availability. Read more: Maritime Industry Urges Trump to Let Jones Act Waiver Expire November 15 Shipbuilders and their allies on Capitol Hill had argued against any extension , saying they have undercut longstanding protectionist mandates they see as critical to bolstering domestic shipbuilding capacity. But oil and chemical companies said the waiver has helped move cargoes of crude, fertilizer and other commodities between US ports efficiently and at lower cost, helping counteract supply disruptions stoked by the war in Iran and refinery damage in Russia. Some 338 voyages have taken place on foreign vessels since Trump first waived Jones Act restrictions in March , including shipments of Texas crude to Pennsylvania and propane to Puerto Rico, according to government data analyzed by the Cato Institute. California has received the majority of shipments, with 23 million barrels of additional products carried to the state compared with 8 million barrels during the same period last year, the White House official said. An additional 90 million barrels of products — mostly refined fuels — have been shipped between US ports since the waiver was first issued, with gasoline, crude oil and renewable fuel being the biggest beneficiaries, according to the official. The current waiver has helped enable the transport of some 13 million barrels of products, more than a third of which has been gasoline, with about 28% crude oil. The waiver’s use, however, has shrunk after Trump limited its scope. Under the new approach, the US Maritime Administration needs to be consulted on the availability of US-flagged, -owned and -operated vessels before the waiver is applied to individual voyages. Products that benefit under the waiver include gasoline, jet fuel, crude oil, naphtha, liquefied natural gas, soy oil and fertilizers. Trump’s Jones Act exemption has been the longest and broadest waiver of the law in more than seven decades. Previous presidents have discretely lifted Jones Act mandates for individual voyages and short periods in the wake of hurricanes and pipeline outages that disrupted fuel flows. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. REUTERS/Christiana Botic TPX IMAGES OF THE DAY All passengers and crew aboard an American Cruise Lines riverboat survived after a Marshall Islands-flagged asphalt tanker struck the docked paddle-wheeler on the Mississippi River in New Orleans on Friday, causing it to capsize and sending people into the water. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno confirmed that everyone aboard the American Heritage had been accounted for following a massive rescue operation. Thirty-two people were taken to local hospitals, including 30 passengers and two police officers, but none suffered critical injuries. “We have zero people unaccounted for, which truly is a miracle on the Mississippi,” Moreno said at a news conference. The 160-meter tanker Atlantic Asphalt struck the U.S.-flagged American Heritage at approximately 12:30 p.m. local time as it was traveling upbound on the Lower Mississippi River, just below the Crescent City Connection bridge, according to the Port of New Orleans. Video of the collision shows the much larger tanker striking the docked paddlewheeler, which began taking on water and listing heavily before eventually capsizing alongside the dock. Other footage shows people in the river wearing life jackets as tugboat operators, nearby vessel crews, police and emergency responders rushed to pull them to safety. The American Heritage had docked outside the Port of New Orleans Administration Building approximately two hours earlier to begin disembarking passengers following an eight-day Mississippi River cruise. Port officials initially reported approximately 129 passengers aboard, in addition to crew members. Moreno said passengers began evacuating after the initial impact, but the vessel overturned before everyone could get off, forcing rescuers to pull people from the water. Louisiana Governor Jeff Landry praised the response, calling the outcome “nothing short of a miracle.” “While we will continue to work through the details of this incident, one thing is clear: our first responders on the national, state, and local level saved countless lives today, and for that I and all of our country are thankful!” Landry said. In an updated statement Friday, American Cruise Lines said it was arranging hotel accommodations and assistance for everyone who had been aboard the American Heritage . “We are getting everyone who was aboard the ship settled into hotels and making sure they have everything they need,” the company said. American Cruise Lines also thanked the U.S. Coast Guard, its crew and local first responders for their rescue efforts, adding that it remained in close contact with the Coast Guard, New Orleans Police and other agencies. The cause of the collision remains under investigation, although the U.S. Coast Guard said the tanker may have experienced a steering failure. Coast Guard Capt. Melanie Burnham said the tanker appeared to have experienced “some type of loss of steering,” but emphasized that the exact cause had not been determined. The National Transportation Safety Board has launched an investigation and is sending a team to New Orleans, with investigators expected to arrive Saturday morning. The Coast Guard also closed the Mississippi River to vessel traffic between mile markers 93 and 96 while emergency operations continued, temporarily disrupting navigation along one of the nation’s busiest commercial waterways. Officials said they were evaluating when the waterway could safely reopen. According to MarineTraffic , the Atlantic Asphalt is a 160-meter asphalt and bitumen tanker sailing under the Marshall Islands flag. The American Heritage is an 81-meter U.S.-flagged paddlewheel cruise ship built in 2015 with accommodations for up to 150 passengers. AIS data shows the Atlantic Asphalt called at Amuay, Venezuela, in October before arriving in Paulsboro, New Jersey. The tanker departed Paulsboro on October 26 and arrived in New Orleans on November 11, two days before the collision. The investigation will focus on what caused the tanker to strike the docked passenger vessel along the busy Lower Mississippi River, where deep-draft oceangoing ships regularly navigate in close proximity to river cruise vessels, tugs and barges. November 13, 2026 © Michael Derrer Fuchs - stock.adobe.com The third quarter of 2026 took place in a volatile economic environment, with persistent tensions in the Middle East impacting international trade and global supply chains. In this context, both shipping and logistics activities were affected by adjustments made to trade routes and transport networks. Nevertheless, the global economy demonstrated relative resilience given the scale of the shock to energy prices, while international trade remained dynamic. The Group’s transported volumes increased by 5.5% compared with the third quarter of 2025, outperforming the market. This represents one of the strongest growth rates recorded in recent years. This growth was underpinned by three key drivers: Restocking , as companies sought to build up inventories amid ongoing economic and geopolitical uncertainty; Increased investment in AI-related infrastructure and data centres; Strong momentum in clean technologies and electric vehicles , particularly in China, amid higher hydrocarbon prices. The CMA CGM Group leveraged the complementary strengths of its shipping, logistics and terminal operations to offer customers integrated solutions across the entire supply chain. This strategy is underpinned by investments in port infrastructure, which are essential to expanding the Group’s capacity and strengthening its global network. The Group also accelerated its transformation through innovation and artificial intelligence across all its businesses. MAIA, its agentic AI platform co-developed with Mistral AI, is being progressively rolled out to employees across its shipping, logistics and media businesses. In France, the CMA CGM Group confirms its long-term commitment and contribution to the country's economic, maritime and logistics development. The Group supports 96,500 jobs, including 19,100 direct jobs and 77,400 jobs across the wider economy. The Group has welcomed the first vessels in its new series of 24,000-TEU containerships, including the CMA CGM NOTRE DAME, CMA CGM PANTHEON and CMA CGM ORSAY, which are deployed on its flagship FAL service connecting Asia and Europe. These are the world's largest LNG-powered containerships operating under the French flag. CMA CGM also accelerated the energy transition in shipping through several major alternative fuel bunkering operations: bioethanol in Brazil, bio-LNG in Rotterdam and a world-record biomethanol bunkering operation in Shanghai. Its presence across the entire logistics chain, the flexibility of its network and the strength of its balance sheet are major assets in order to cope with changes in its operating environment and provide long-term support to its customers.
